summary: Reviewed the dvpwa aiohttp application: DAO layer (sqli/dao/*), request handlers (sqli/views.py), auth/session/CSRF utilities and middlewares, Jinja2 setup and templates, configuration, and DB bootstrap. The app is a deliberately vulnerable teaching project and the overall risk is critical: an unauthenticated SQL injection, stored XSS enabled by disabled autoescaping, disabled CSRF protection, missing server-side authorization on state-changing endpoints, and weak MD5 password hashing are all present and reachable. Static assets and migration schema were only skimmed.

findings.title: SQL injection in Student.create via string-formatted INSERT
findings.description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement by interpolating the student name directly into the SQL string with Python % formatting, instead of passing it as a query parameter. The name comes straight from unauthenticated user input: views.students() reads data['name'] from a POST to /students/ (no auth, and CSRF is disabled) and passes it to Student.create. An attacker can break out of the quoted VALUES literal and inject arbitrary SQL (e.g. name = "x'); DROP TABLE marks; --" or stacked/sub-query payloads), enabling data exfiltration or modification.
findings.evidence: student.py: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name}); await cur.execute(q). Source: views.py:57 await Student.create(conn, data['name']) where data = await request.post() on POST /students/. Contrast with the parameterized create methods in course.py/review.py/mark.py which pass params to cur.execute.
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query: await cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never build SQL with %/format/f-strings on user input.

findings.title: Autoescaping disabled in Jinja2 enables stored XSS in course/review templates
findings.description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so any template variable rendered without an explicit | e filter is emitted as raw HTML. Several templates render attacker-controlled, persisted data unescaped: course.jinja2 outputs course.title and course.description ({{ course.title }} line 14, {{ course.description }} line 15) and each review.review_text ({{ review.review_text }} line 22); student.jinja2 outputs course.title/description (lines 19-20). review_text and course title/description are stored via unauthenticated POST endpoints (/courses/{id}/review and /courses/), so an attacker can store <script> payloads that execute in any viewer's browser (including the admin). Because session cookies are not HttpOnly, this leads to session hijacking.
findings.evidence: app.py: setup_jinja(app, loader=..., context_processors=[...], autoescape=False). Sinks: course.jinja2:14-15,22; student.jinja2:19-20. Sources: views.review() -> Review.create(conn, course_id, review_text) with review_text from request.post(); views.courses() -> Course.create(conn, data['title'], data['description']).
findings.recommendation: Enable autoescaping (autoescape=True, or autoescape=select_autoescape(['html','jinja2'])) and remove reliance on manual | e. Keep explicit escaping as defense in depth.

findings.title: CSRF protection middleware disabled for all state-changing POST routes
findings.description: The csrf_middleware (which validates a per-session _csrf_token on POST) is commented out of the application's middleware list, so none of the POST endpoints enforce CSRF tokens. All state-changing actions - login (POST /), create student, create course, submit review, and evaluate/grade a student - accept cross-site forged requests. An attacker can host a page that auto-submits a form to these endpoints and act on behalf of a logged-in victim (e.g. an admin), including creating content with XSS payloads.
findings.evidence: app.py middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware]. The csrf_middleware exists and is correct (middlewares.py:25-38) but is never registered. Routes POST / , /students/, /courses/, /students/{..}/evaluate/{..}, /courses/{..}/review (routes.py) are thus unprotected.
findings.recommendation: Re-enable csrf_middleware in the middleware chain and ensure every POST form includes the csrf_token hidden field (most templates already emit it).

findings.title: Missing server-side authorization on state-changing endpoints (student grading, content creation)
findings.description: The evaluate handler assigns marks/grades to students but performs no authorization check - any anonymous client can POST to /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id} and set a student's points. The UI only shows the evaluate form to admins ({% if auth_user.is_admin %} in course.jinja2:41), but this client-side gating is not enforced on the server. The same missing-authorization pattern applies to views.students (create student, views.py:51-60), views.courses (create course, views.py:83-93), and views.review (create review, views.py:111-131): none use the existing @authorize decorator, so all write operations are fully anonymous. Only logout is protected (views.py:156).
findings.evidence: evaluate() has no @authorize/@authorize(ensure_admin=True) decorator and no is_admin check before Mark.create(conn, student_id, course_id, data['points']). The authorize() decorator in utils/auth.py:12-23 supports ensure_admin but is unused on these handlers. Compare course.jinja2:41 which hides the form behind auth_user.is_admin.
findings.recommendation: Apply @authorize(ensure_admin=True) to evaluate (and any admin-only action) and @authorize() to other write handlers, enforcing permissions server-side rather than only in templates.

findings.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 and compared non-constant-time
findings.description: User.check_password hashes the supplied password with a single unsalted MD5 and compares it to the stored hash. MD5 is fast and broken for password storage: stored hashes (also seeded as md5('...') in migrations/001-fixtures.sql) are trivially cracked via rainbow tables/brute force, and lack of per-user salt means identical passwords yield identical hashes. The comparison with == is also not constant-time, allowing theoretical timing analysis.
findings.evidence: user.py: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest(); fixtures: md5('superadmin'), md5('password'), md5('spidey').
findings.recommendation: Use a slow, salted password hash (bcrypt/scrypt/argon2) via a vetted library, and compare using a constant-time function (e.g. the library's verify). Rehash existing credentials on next login.

findings.title: Session cookies issued without HttpOnly flag
findings.description: The RedisStorage session backend is instantiated with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable from JavaScript (document.cookie). Combined with the stored XSS enabled by disabled autoescaping, an attacker's injected script can exfiltrate the session cookie and hijack authenticated (including admin) sessions.
findings.recommendation: Remove httponly=False (default is True) and also set secure=True and an appropriate samesite policy for the session cookie.

findings.title: Application runs with debug mode enabled
findings.description: The aiohttp Application is created with debug=True unconditionally. Debug mode enables extra diagnostics and more verbose error behavior, which can leak internal details and increases attack surface in production. It is hard-coded rather than driven by configuration/environment.
findings.recommendation: Drive debug from configuration/environment and default it to False in production deployments.
